title: Trust Your Naseeb: Stop Worrying About What Allah Has Already Written
content:
Recently, I was reading the translation of Surah Al-Hadid, particularly verses 22 and 23, and something about their meaning stayed with me.

Allah says:

مَا أَصَابَ مِن مُّصِيبَةٍ فِي الْأَرْضِ وَلَا فِي أَنفُسِكُمْ إِلَّا فِي كِتَابٍ مِّن قَبْلِ أَن نَّبْرَأَهَا

“No disaster strikes upon the earth or among yourselves except that it is in a register before We bring it into being...” (Qur'an 57:22)

And in the following verse, Allah tells us not to grieve excessively over what has passed us by or become arrogant over what we have been given.

It made me think about how much time we spend worrying about things that are not even in our control. We regret what we couldn't keep, question why certain things didn't happen, and become anxious about a future we haven't experienced.

Sometimes, we spend so much time asking ourselves What if things go wrong? that we forget to consider that perhaps things might turn out better than we ever imagined.

This is where trusting your naseeb becomes meaningful.

We make plans, develop expectations, become attached to certain people, and imagine how our lives should unfold. But life doesn't always follow the direction we choose. Some opportunities disappear, some relationships don't last, and some prayers take longer than we expected.

And when things don't happen according to our wishes, we often find ourselves questioning everything.

But perhaps we need to remind ourselves that not everything we want is necessarily what is best for us, and not everything we lose is necessarily a loss.

Trusting Allah's decree doesn't mean giving up on your dreams or sitting back without making an effort. It means working towards what you want while understanding that the final outcome is not yours to control. Make your efforts, pray sincerely, and leave the rest to the One who knows what you cannot see.

Think about Prophet Musa (AS). When he left Egypt, he had no clear picture of what his future would look like. He eventually reached Madyan, where he helped two women and then turned to Allah with this beautiful dua:

رَبِّ إِنِّي لِمَا أَنزَلْتَ إِلَيَّ مِنْ خَيْرٍ فَقِيرٌ

“My Lord, indeed I am in need of whatever good You would send down to me.” (Qur'an 28:24)

He didn't know what would happen next, but Allah opened doors for him that he could never have planned himself.

Sometimes, we are standing at a point in our lives where we can only see uncertainty, while the future holds possibilities we haven't even considered.

And there is another thing we need to learn: stop living in the past.

We cannot change the conversations we wish had gone differently, the opportunities we missed, the decisions we regret, or the people who are no longer part of our lives. We can learn from these experiences, but continuously punishing ourselves for them will not change what has already happened.

Allah reminds us:

وَلَا تَيْأَسُوا مِن رَّوْحِ اللَّهِ

“And despair not of relief from Allah.” (Qur'an 12:87)

These words were spoken by Prophet Yaqub (AS), who experienced profound grief over his separation from Yusuf (AS). His story teaches us that sadness and faith are not opposites. You can miss something, feel disappointed, and still have hope in Allah.

So, the next time you find yourself worrying about what is coming, remember that you don't need to figure out your entire future today.

Keep making dua. Keep working towards your goals. Appreciate the people and blessings you have right now. And when something doesn't happen the way you wanted, don't immediately assume that your life is going in the wrong direction.

Perhaps one day, you will understand why certain doors remained closed and why other paths opened when you least expected them.

Your job is to make the effort, place your trust in Allah, and remain hopeful.

Don't let yesterday's regrets or tomorrow's uncertainties take away the peace of today. What Allah has written for you is not beyond His reach, and what you cannot see today is already known to Him.

Trust your naseeb.

title: Even When I Lose My Enthusiasm, God Still Wakes Me Up Every Morning
content:
There are days when I lose my enthusiasm for almost everything. Days when the things that once excited me feel ordinary, when the future seems uncertain, and when even the smallest efforts require more strength than I seem to have. Sometimes, I find myself questioning my direction, wondering whether all the things I hope for will ever become reality.

Yet, despite all those thoughts, another morning arrives.

The sun rises, the world continues moving, and somehow, I open my eyes again. Another day is placed before me, even when I have no idea what to do with it. And perhaps there is something deeply meaningful about that.

I often think about how easily we overlook the significance of being given another day. We become so occupied with what we haven't achieved, what we have lost, and what remains beyond our reach that we forget to appreciate the opportunity that still exists in front of us.

We measure our lives through accomplishments, milestones, relationships, recognition, and material success. When these things do not happen according to our expectations, we begin to feel as though life has stopped moving in our favour. We lose enthusiasm, compare our circumstances with others, and sometimes convince ourselves that we are falling behind.

But perhaps we are looking at life through a very narrow window.

Not every meaningful thing happens when we expect it to. Not every unanswered prayer is a forgotten prayer. Not every delay is a denial, and not every difficult chapter is the conclusion of our story.

There is a certain comfort in believing that Allah, in His infinite wisdom, knows what we cannot see. We may not understand why certain doors remain closed, why some opportunities never arrive, or why the things we sincerely wish for take so long. But our inability to understand the timing of something does not mean that our lives have lost their purpose.

Sometimes, faith is not about waking up every morning feeling motivated, optimistic, or completely certain about the future. Sometimes, faith is simply continuing to trust Allah when your enthusiasm has disappeared and your circumstances offer very little reason for optimism.

And that is what makes another morning so meaningful to me.

It reminds me that I am still here. That there are still things to learn, people to meet, experiences to live, mistakes to correct, prayers to make, and possibilities I have not yet encountered.

Perhaps the fortune I keep waiting for has not reached me yet. Perhaps the opportunities I have been hoping for are still somewhere ahead. Or perhaps the life I am meant to appreciate is already unfolding in ways I have not learned to recognize.

I do not know what tomorrow holds, and neither can I claim that everything will eventually happen exactly as I wish. Life does not promise us that. But I can choose not to treat today's uncertainty as proof that tomorrow holds nothing for me.

So, even when I lose my enthusiasm, I want to remember one thing: Allah has allowed me to witness another morning.

And perhaps that is enough reason to try again.

title: See the good in everything, and the good will look for you too
content:
There is something beautiful about a person who manages to find goodness in a world that constantly gives them reasons to become bitter.

Life is rarely as simple as we imagine it to be. People disappoint us, plans fall apart, opportunities disappear, and sometimes things happen that leave us questioning everything. We encounter situations we never asked for, experience losses we never prepared for, and meet people who teach us lessons we wish we had never needed to learn.

Yet, somewhere between all these experiences, we develop a choice: to allow everything that happens to us to change us for the worse, or to preserve the ability to see something good even in imperfect circumstances.

I believe the way we look at life has a significant influence on the way we experience it.

Consider two people facing the same difficult situation. One sees nothing but disappointment, while the other tries to understand what the experience might teach them. Their circumstances are identical, but their perspectives are different. One becomes trapped in what went wrong; the other leaves room for what might still go right.

This does not mean pretending that pain does not exist, forcing ourselves to smile when we are hurting, or finding excuses for people who treat us poorly. Some things genuinely hurt. Some experiences are unfair, and some situations deserve to be acknowledged rather than romanticized.

But there is a difference between recognizing the darkness around us and allowing it to become the only thing we see.

When we constantly search for reasons to complain, we eventually begin noticing everything that goes wrong. We become so familiar with disappointment that even good experiences start feeling ordinary. We overlook kindness, underestimate small blessings, and forget how much there is to appreciate in an otherwise imperfect life.

The opposite is also true. When we consciously look for goodness, we become more attentive to it. A sincere conversation, an unexpected act of kindness, a peaceful morning, a lesson hidden inside a difficult experience, or simply having another opportunity to begin again can become meaningful.

Perhaps this is what it means to see the good in everything. Not that everything is good, but that goodness can still exist alongside things that are not.

And I think this perspective also changes the way we treat other people. When we approach the world with goodwill, we are more likely to offer kindness without constantly calculating what we will receive in return. We become less interested in competing with everyone, less occupied with resentment, and more willing to appreciate people for who they are.

Of course, the world will not always return that kindness. Not everyone will understand your intentions, appreciate your efforts, or treat you with the same consideration. Seeing the good in people should never mean abandoning your boundaries or ignoring their actions.

Still, I would rather preserve a heart that can recognize goodness than develop one that has become suspicious of everything.

Perhaps the good does not always look for us in the literal sense. Perhaps it is not a matter of the universe rewarding every positive thought with a positive outcome. Rather, when we develop a habit of looking for goodness, we become better at recognizing opportunities, appreciating people, and finding meaning in experiences we might otherwise overlook.

And sometimes, that changes more about our lives than we realize.

So, see the good in everything. Not because life is always beautiful, but because there is already enough disappointment in the world without us choosing to contribute more of it.

Be kind, remain hopeful, appreciate the little things, and never allow a few unpleasant experiences to convince you that goodness no longer exists.

The world may not always give you reasons to smile, but don't let it take away your ability to find them.

title: The Architecture of Unexamined Assumptions
subtitle: Why the ideas we are most certain of are often the ones we understand least.
content:
It is surprisingly easy to live inside an intellectual house without ever inspecting its foundations. We inherit ideas from parents, mentors, social circles, and the prevailing ethos of our era. Over time, these adopted perspectives harden into what feels like self-evident common sense.

We rarely stop to ask: How did this belief get here? What evidence would it take for me to abandon it?

The Comfort of Intellectual Inertia

Questioning one's fundamental assumptions is genuinely uncomfortable. It induces a mild vertigo. If the premise upon which you constructed an argument turns out to be fragile, everything built upon it suddenly trembles.

Because the human brain is an energy-conserving organ, it naturally prefers coherence over truth. Once an overarching narrative is established, it filters out discordant observations and welcomes confirmatory evidence with open arms.

Certainty is not a measure of truth; it is merely an emotional state of cognitive closure.

The Discipline of Looking Twice

In computer science, when a system behaves unexpectedly, our first instinct is often to blame the external library or the operating system. But in nine cases out of ten, the flaw lies in an implicit assumption we wrote into our own algorithm—an assumption so obvious that we forgot we made it.

The same principle governs our worldview. Whether thinking about politics, morality, or our own personal capabilities, the most rewarding intellectual exercise is often to take our most cherished conclusions and deliberate against them with full intellectual vigor.

Not every exploration leads to discarding what we believe. Sometimes, testing an assumption reveals that it is rock-solid. But now, it is no longer an inherited prejudice; it is an understood conviction.

title: On Cognitive Rabbit Holes and Serendipitous Learning
subtitle: How straying outside specialization enriches our understanding of everything.
content:
Specialization is the prevailing currency of modern professional life. We are urged to pick a lane, narrow our focus, and develop deep, defensible expertise. There is unquestionable utility in this advice—complex engineering systems and medical breakthroughs require extraordinary depth.

Yet, something vital is sacrificed when we treat our intellectual curiosity like an industrial pipeline rather than an ecosystem.

The Unplanned Detour

Some of the most illuminating connections I have encountered occurred not while diligently studying algorithms or data structures, but while wandering through unrelated domains—reading about historical political fractures, the neurobiology of perception, or classical philosophical debates on personal identity.

When you read outside your primary domain, concepts do not remain isolated. They cross-pollinate. A concept from evolutionary biology sheds unexpected light on how distributed networks handle consensus. An ancient philosophical dispute about free will alters how you contemplate artificial cognition.

Curiosity is not a distraction from serious work; it is the raw material that makes serious work fertile.

Learning Without an Immediate Transaction

Too much of contemporary education is transactional: we learn something so we can pass an examination, land a role, or impress an audience. But the purest joy of reading is non-transactional—reading simply because something caught your attention and made you want to know how it works.

This publication is built around that premise. It is a home for the questions that linger after the textbooks are closed.
